learn.title: Choosing a sort
learn.body: Every sort so far gives the same sorted result, but cost and behaviour differ. This lesson compares them and meets a new idea: stability.

learn.title: The costs
learn.body: Bubble and selection sort: $\Theta(n^2)$ comparisons. Insertion sort: $O(n^2)$ worst, $O(n)$ best. Merge sort: $O(n \log n)$ always, but needs an extra array of size n. For small arrays the simple sorts are fine. For large ones merge sort wins.

learn.title: What is stability
learn.body: A sort is stable if equal items keep their original order. This matters when sorting records. Sort students by grade: with a stable sort, two students with the same grade stay in the order they were already in, for example alphabetical.

learn.title: Selection versus insertion on equal keys
learn.body: Sort {2a, 2b, 1c} by the number only. Two items share the key 2.
steps: Selection sort swaps 2a with the smallest, 1c: 1c 2b 2a
The two 2s changed order, so selection sort is not stable
The two 2s kept their order, so insertion sort is stable

learn.title: The idea of quicksort
learn.body: Quicksort picks an item called the pivot. It moves smaller items to its left and larger ones to its right, so the pivot is in its final place. Then it sorts the left and right parts the same way. On average it is $O(n \log n)$ and it needs little extra memory.

learn.title: When quicksort struggles
learn.body: If the pivot is always the smallest or largest item, one side is empty and the other has nearly all the items. That happens, for example, when the first item is the pivot and the array is already sorted. The cost becomes $O(n^2)$. Good pivot choices avoid it.

choices: equal items keep their original order
questions.explanation: Stability is about the order of equal keys.

questions.prompt: Which of these sorts, as written in this unit, is stable?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort only moves items past strictly bigger ones, so equal items never cross. Selection sort's long-distance swaps can reorder equal items.

questions.prompt: {2a, 2b, 1c} sorted by number with selection sort gives...
Merge sort always costs $O(n \log n)$ but needs an extra \_\_.
questions.explanation: The output of each merge is written into extra space.

questions.prompt: In quicksort, the pivot ends up...
questions.explanation: Smaller items are left of it, larger are right, so its position is settled.

questions.prompt: Match each sort to its cost.
questions.explanation: The cost depends on the algorithm and sometimes on the input.

questions.prompt: Which input can make quicksort slow, with the first item as the pivot?
questions.explanation: Each pivot is the smallest remaining item, so one side is always empty.
